discussion.prompt: A box stands for the number of marbles in a bag. What does the box represent?
steps: It represents a quantity, not the bag’s name or colour.
If marbles are added, the quantity represented by the box changes. Draw your own symbol.

discussion.prompt: In “□ + 3 = 8”, explain what □ means without guessing randomly.
steps: The box is the unknown part. Count up from 3 to 8 to find it.
Five is the amount that makes both sides equal; putting it back checks the meaning.

discussion.prompt: A menu writes n for the number of apples chosen. Explain n for zero apples and for four apples.
steps: The same symbol can stand for different chosen quantities in different situations.
Here n is 0 or 4; it is not a multiplication sign or a unit of money.

discussion.prompt: Write a number story in which a symbol stands for how many counters are hidden.
steps: Choose the total and show the visible counters.
Use the symbol for the hidden part, and explain how uncovering the counters checks the story.

title: Sequential, concurrent, and repeating code · another way
Read and alter repeating events · explore

discussion.prompt: Plan fair places for 9 children at tables that each seat 4. Draw a plan.
steps: Name what is known and what you need to find. Try tables with counters for children.
Two tables seat 8, so one child still needs a place. A third table works; discuss the empty seats.
Check your plan with a partner, then revise it if two more children arrive.

discussion.prompt: Plan a snack for 12 children when each plate holds 5 pieces of fruit.
steps: Decide whether each child needs one piece, and state that assumption.
Draw two full plates and the extra pieces; a third plate is needed if nobody shares a piece.
Test and revise the plan if some children do not want fruit.

discussion.prompt: Design a quiet reading corner for 6 children. What information do you need?
steps: Choose assumptions about space, seating, and safe walking paths.
Make a drawing and use counters to test whether everyone fits.
Explain a change that makes the model work better. There can be more than one sensible plan.

discussion.prompt: Plan how to share 10 crayons between two tables with different numbers of learners.
steps: Decide whether fairness means equal crayons per table or enough colours for each learner.
Draw a first plan and check it against your chosen rule.
Discuss the assumptions and revise the plan when the group sizes change.

discussion.prompt: Survey both favourite fruit and how learners travel to school. How can a two-way table help?
steps: Use fruit as rows and travel as columns; put each response in exactly one matching cell.
Check the row and column totals against the number of learners interviewed.

discussion.prompt: Choose a question involving categories and another involving counts. Explain how to record both.
steps: A favourite colour is a category; a number of books is a count.
Use consistent questions and organize the observations in a labelled frequency table.

title: Compare means and modes · another way

discussion.prompt: Build a small box from blocks. Which flat shapes can you see on its outside?
steps: Turn the structure to look at the top, front, and sides.
Trace a flat face on paper and compare the outline with a square or rectangle.

discussion.prompt: Use two blocks and a cylinder to build a model. Describe its parts.
steps: Identify each solid before joining the parts.
Point to a flat face and a curved surface. Building a model is a hands-on task.

title: Structures and component shapes · another way

discussion.prompt: Build a structure from a cube, rectangular prism, and cone. Identify its parts before taking it apart.
steps: Describe the solids and the shapes of the faces where parts touch.
Rebuild the same structure and explain which parts were moved.

discussion.prompt: Draw a shape using equal square tiles, then rearrange all the tiles.
steps: Count every tile once and avoid gaps or overlaps.
Explain why the area is unchanged even if the new shape looks longer.

discussion.prompt: Two cube models use the same edge length. Turn one cube. Can they still match?
steps: Match a face and its edges without stretching either model.
A turn changes position, not size or shape. The models can be congruent.

discussion.prompt: A cube and a larger cube look alike. Are they congruent?
steps: Compare their corresponding edge lengths and square faces.
Their sizes differ, so the faces cannot cover one another exactly.

discussion.prompt: Build two rectangular prisms from identical blocks in the same arrangement. Compare their faces.
steps: Place corresponding faces together and compare their lengths and corners.
Matching the whole objects requires the same shape and size, not just the same block count.

discussion.prompt: Two structures contain six cubes each but have different arrangements. Must they be congruent?
steps: An equal number of pieces does not guarantee an identical outer shape.
Try turning the models to match every part. If the arrangements cannot match, they are not congruent.

title: Multistep directions and turns · another way

discussion.prompt: A learner measures with blocks but leaves gaps. What happens to the count?
steps: Gaps leave part of the length or area unmeasured, so too few units may be counted.
Start again with equal units touching without gaps or overlaps.

discussion.prompt: Two learners fill a jug. One uses level scoops and one overfills every scoop. Is the comparison fair?
steps: The scoops are no longer equal units. Overfilled scoops can give a smaller scoop count for the same jug.
Use a level scoop consistently and compare the results again.

title: Mass on a pan balance · another way
Different units, same attribute · another way

discussion.prompt: A learner covers a shape with overlapping tiles. Does the tile count give its area accurately?
steps: Overlaps count some surface more than once.
Fit equal tiles without gaps or overlaps, then count again.

discussion.prompt: You measure the same length with paper clips and larger blocks. Why do the counts differ?
steps: A larger unit covers more of the unchanged length, so fewer units are needed.
Name both the count and the unit; the object itself has not changed size.
